content.text: Chapter 5, Work, Energy and Power, develops the scalar product, work and kinetic energy, the work-energy theorem, variable-force work, potential energy, conservation of mechanical energy, spring potential energy, power, and collisions.

The scalar (dot) product of vectors A and B is a scalar equal to the product of their magnitudes and the cosine of the angle between them. It equals the magnitude of one vector multiplied by the component of the other along it.

For vectors expressed in Cartesian components, the dot product is the sum of products of corresponding components. A vector dotted with itself gives the square of its magnitude; perpendicular vectors have zero dot product.
The dot product is commutative and distributive over vector addition, and scalar multiplication can be taken outside the dot product.
The Cartesian unit vectors have unit dot products with themselves and zero dot products with each other.

For F = (3î + 4ĵ − 5k̂) and d = (5î + 4ĵ + 3k̂), F·d = 16. Since F·d = |F||d|cosθ and both magnitudes are √50, cosθ = 16/50 = 0.32; the angle is cos⁻¹(0.32). The projection-related scalar product is 16 in the stated units.

metadata.topic: Worked example 5.1: force and displacement vectors

content.text: Starting from v²−u² = 2a·d and multiplying by m/2 gives the change in kinetic energy equal to the work done by the net force. The relation generalises to vector motion.
Kinetic energy is the scalar quantity associated with motion. For mass m and velocity v, it equals one half mass times speed squared; its SI unit is joule.

The work-energy theorem states that the change in a particle’s kinetic energy equals the work done on it by the net force. It is an integral/scalar form of Newton’s second law and does not retain all instantaneous directional information.

A 1.00 g drop falling 1.00 km reaches 50.0 m s⁻¹. Assuming it starts from rest and g = 10 m s⁻², its kinetic-energy increase is 1.25 J, gravity does 10.0 J of work, and the resistive force does −8.75 J.
For a constant force F and displacement d, work is the dot product of force and displacement. Only the component of force along the displacement contributes.

Work is zero if displacement is zero, the force is zero, or force and displacement are perpendicular. A person holding a load stationary does no work on the load; gravity does no work on ideal horizontal motion.
Work is positive when the force has a component along displacement and negative when it opposes displacement. Friction opposing motion commonly does negative work.
Work and energy have dimensions [ML²T⁻²] and SI unit joule (J). Alternative units are listed in the chapter’s Table 5.1.

A cyclist skids to a stop over 10 m while the road exerts a 200 N force opposite the motion. The road does −2000 J of work on the cycle. The cycle does zero work on the road in this example because the road’s displacement is zero.
Kinetic energy measures the work an object can do by virtue of its motion. Examples in the chapter include flowing water, wind, and moving bullets.
A 50.0 g bullet enters plywood at 200 m s⁻¹ and emerges with 10% of its initial kinetic energy. Its initial kinetic energy is 1000 J, final kinetic energy is 100 J, and emergent speed is 63.2 m s⁻¹.

For a force varying with position, divide displacement into small intervals where the force is approximately constant. Work is the limiting sum of F(x)Δx, equal to the signed area under the force-displacement graph.

The woman applies 100 N over the first 10 m, then her force decreases linearly to 50 N over the next 10 m. Work by her force is the rectangle plus trapezium area, 1750 J. A constant 50 N opposing friction force does −1000 J over 20 m.
In one dimension, using Newton’s second law, dK/dt = Fv and therefore dK = F dx. Integration yields the change in kinetic energy equal to the integral of force over displacement.
equations: Kf − Ki = ∫(xi to xf) F dx = W

content.text: A 1 kg block enters a rough patch at 2 m s⁻¹. In 0.1 < x < 2.01 m the retarding force is −k/x with k = 0.5 J, and zero outside. Integrating the force gives final kinetic energy 0.5 J and final speed 1 m s⁻¹.
Potential energy is stored energy associated with position or configuration. For a conservative force, work done against the force can be stored and later appear as kinetic energy.

Taking the ground as zero potential energy and treating g as constant near Earth, an object of mass m at height h has gravitational potential energy mgh. Gravitational force is the negative derivative of this potential.
A potential-energy function V(x) can be defined for a conservative force when F(x) = −dV/dx. Work by such a force depends only on initial and final positions; work around a closed path is zero.
For a system acted on only by conservative forces, the sum of kinetic and potential energy remains constant. Kinetic and potential energy can change individually while their sum is conserved.
For a ball dropped from height H, the initial energy is mgH. At height h, energy is mgh + ½mvh², and at ground level it is ½mvf². Thus vf = √(2gH) and vh² = 2g(H−h).

A bob on a string of length L is given horizontal speed v0 at the lowest point and reaches the top just as the string becomes slack. At the top, tension is zero and vc² = gL. Energy conservation gives v0² = 5gL, vB² = 3gL, and KB/KC = 3. At the top, the bob’s velocity is horizontal; if released, it follows projectile motion.

content.text: For an ideal spring, the restoring force is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed oppositely. The spring constant k has unit N m⁻¹; large k means a stiff spring.

The work done by the spring force in moving from equilibrium to displacement x is negative and equals −kx²/2. Between any two positions, it depends only on the endpoints, and work over a complete cycle is zero.

Taking zero potential energy at equilibrium, the spring potential energy at extension or compression x is ½kx². In an ideal mass-spring system, kinetic and potential energies trade off while total mechanical energy stays constant.

A 1000 kg car moving at 18 km h⁻¹ (5 m s⁻¹) strikes a spring with k = 5.25 × 10³ N m⁻¹ on a smooth road. At maximum compression, kinetic energy becomes spring potential energy, giving maximum compression xm = 2.00 m.

metadata.topic: Worked example 5.8: car compressing a spring

content.text: Friction is non-conservative; its work depends on the path and mechanical energy is not conserved by itself. For conservative and non-conservative forces together, the change in mechanical energy equals work by non-conservative forces.

With coefficient of friction 0.5, friction and spring force both oppose compression. The work-energy theorem gives a quadratic equation for maximum compression; the chapter obtains xm = 1.35 m, smaller than the frictionless result.

content.text: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy. Average power is work divided by elapsed time; instantaneous power is the time derivative of work. Power is scalar, has dimensions [ML²T⁻³], and SI unit watt (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). One horsepower is 746 W.
A 100 W bulb operating for 10 hours uses 1 kWh. Kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

An elevator of total mass 1800 kg rises at constant speed 2 m s⁻¹ against 4000 N friction. With g = 10 m s⁻², the motor must supply 22,000 N upward force, so minimum power is 44,000 W, approximately 59 hp.

During a collision, the mutual impulsive forces are equal and opposite by Newton’s third law. For an isolated two-body system, the total linear momentum is conserved even though kinetic energy may be converted to heat, sound, or deformation.

In an elastic collision, total linear momentum and total kinetic energy before and after the collision are conserved. In an inelastic collision, momentum remains conserved for an isolated system but some initial kinetic energy is transformed into other forms. In a completely inelastic collision, bodies move together after impact.
For a moving mass m1 with initial speed v1i colliding with stationary mass m2 and then moving together, momentum conservation gives the common final speed.
For a one-dimensional elastic collision where m1 moves initially and m2 is at rest, conservation of momentum and kinetic energy gives the final velocities shown below.

For equal masses in a one-dimensional elastic collision, the first mass stops and the second moves with the initial speed of the first. If the target mass is much greater than the incoming mass, the light mass approximately reverses velocity while the heavy mass remains nearly at rest.

The chapter shows that elastic collisions with light nuclei can transfer much of a neutron’s kinetic energy. The fractional energy remaining with the neutron is [(m1−m2)/(m1+m2)]²; the fraction transferred to the moderator is 4m1m2/(m1+m2)². For deuterium, m2 = 2m1, the neutron retains 1/9 and transfers 8/9 of its initial kinetic energy.

For a collision where one body initially moves along x and the other is at rest, conservation of momentum applies separately to x and y components. For elastic collisions, kinetic energy conservation provides an additional equation; enough known quantities are needed to determine final speeds and angles.
For equal-mass billiard balls in an elastic glancing collision, with the target initially at rest, the two final velocities are perpendicular. If the target’s direction is θ2 = 37°, then θ1 = 53°.
Work is the scalar product of force and displacement; it may be positive, negative, or zero. Kinetic energy is ½mv². The work-energy theorem relates net work to change in kinetic energy.

Potential energy is defined for conservative forces. Gravitational potential energy near Earth is mgh and spring potential energy is ½kx². Mechanical energy K+V is conserved when only conservative forces do work; with non-conservative forces, its change equals their work.

content.text: Power is the rate of doing work, with instantaneous value F·v. In collisions, total momentum is conserved for an isolated system. Kinetic energy is conserved in elastic collisions but not generally in inelastic collisions.

The chapter stresses that work must be attributed to a specified force and displacement; work is scalar and may be negative. Mutual forces need not do equal-and-opposite work. The work-energy theorem is related to Newton’s second law. Potential energy is defined up to an arbitrary constant and is not associated with every force. In collisions, momentum is conserved throughout an isolated collision, while kinetic-energy conservation for an elastic collision refers to before and after, not every instant of contact.

Determine the sign of work done in each case: a man lifting a bucket by a rope; gravity on the bucket; friction on a body sliding down an incline; an applied force moving a body uniformly on a rough horizontal plane; and air resistance bringing a vibrating pendulum to rest.

A 2 kg body initially at rest is acted on by a horizontal 7 N force on a table with kinetic-friction coefficient 0.1. Calculate work by the applied force, work by friction, net work, and change in kinetic energy over 10 s, and interpret the results.

For the potential-energy functions shown in Fig. 5.11, identify regions inaccessible to a particle at the indicated total energy, state the minimum total energy required in each case, and suggest physical contexts.
For simple harmonic motion with V(x)=kx²/2 and k=0.5 N m⁻¹, show that a particle with total energy 1 J turns back at x=±2 m.

Explain: the energy source for a rocket casing burning from friction; why gravity does zero work over a comet’s complete orbit; why a satellite can speed up while losing energy and approaching Earth; and compare work in two illustrated carrying/pulling situations.

Choose the correct alternatives about how potential energy changes under positive conservative-force work, energy lost against friction, the external force governing total momentum change, and conserved quantities in an inelastic collision.

State true or false with reasons: whether each body’s momentum and energy are conserved in elastic collision; whether total energy is conserved irrespective of forces; whether work over a closed loop is zero for every force; and whether inelastic collisions always reduce total kinetic energy.

Discuss whether kinetic energy and linear momentum are conserved during contact in elastic and inelastic billiard-ball collisions, and classify a collision when the interaction potential depends only on separation.
A body starts from rest and moves in one dimension with constant acceleration. Select the time dependence of power from t^(1/2), t, t^(3/2), or t².
A body moves in one direction under a source of constant power. Select the proportionality of displacement to time from t^(1/2), t, t^(3/2), or t².
A body constrained to move along the z-axis experiences constant force F = −î + 2ĵ + 3k̂ N. Find work when it moves 4 m along the z-axis.
An electron has kinetic energy 10 keV and a proton 100 keV. Determine which is faster and find the ratio of speeds using the given masses and conversion 1 eV = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ J.

A raindrop of radius 2 mm falls 500 m, reaches terminal speed halfway down, then moves uniformly, and reaches ground at 10 m s⁻¹. Find gravitational work over each half and resistive-force work over the whole journey.
A gas molecule hits a horizontal wall at 200 m s⁻¹ and 30° to the normal, then rebounds at the same speed. Is momentum conserved? Is the collision elastic or inelastic?
A pump fills a 30 m³ tank 40 m above ground in 15 min. With efficiency 30%, determine the electric power consumed.
Three identical ball bearings on a frictionless table undergo a head-on collision as shown in Fig. 5.14. For an elastic collision, identify which illustrated result is possible.
A pendulum bob released from 30° to the vertical hits an identical stationary bob in an elastic collision. Find how high the first bob rises after collision.
A pendulum of length 1.5 m is released from horizontal and dissipates 5% of initial energy to air resistance. Find its speed at the lowest point.
A 300 kg trolley carrying a 25 kg sandbag moves at 27 km h⁻¹ on a frictionless track. Sand leaks at 0.05 kg s⁻¹. Find trolley speed after the bag empties.
A 0.5 kg body has velocity v=ax^(3/2), with a=5 m⁻¹/² s⁻¹. Find net work from x=0 to x=2 m.

For a windmill with swept area A and perpendicular wind speed v, find air mass passing in time t and its kinetic energy. For A=30 m², v=36 km h⁻¹, density 1.2 kg m⁻³ and 25% conversion efficiency, find electrical power.
A person lifts a 10 kg mass 1000 times by 0.5 m each time. Find work against gravity and fat used if fat provides 3.8×10⁷ J kg⁻¹ and conversion efficiency is 20%.
A family uses 8 kW. Solar power incident is 200 W m⁻² and 20% is converted to useful electricity. Find required area and compare it with a typical house roof.
